name: Tourmaline
physical: Linked to a sense of balanced energy
Kept nearby for comfort during stress
summary: Tourmaline is the rainbow family of stones, from black schorl to pink rubellite and green verdelite, loved for balance, protection and creative energy.
intro: Tourmaline is a complex boron silicate that crystallizes in long, striated prisms with a rounded triangular cross-section. It comes in more colors than almost any other gem, from black schorl and brown dravite to pink rubellite, green verdelite, blue indicolite, and glowing neon-blue paraiba. One crystal can even shift color along its length, as in watermelon tourmaline, which is pink inside and green outside. Tourmaline is also pyroelectric and piezoelectric, meaning it can develop a static charge when heated or pressed, a quality that fascinated early naturalists. It is found in pegmatites around the world, and Brazil, Afghanistan, and Mozambique produce the best gem material.
history: The name tourmaline comes from the Sinhalese word turmali, used in Sri Lanka for a mixed group of colored stones. Dutch traders in the early eighteenth century brought tourmalines to Europe and noticed that they attracted ash when heated, calling them ash-drawers. In the nineteenth century, Maine's pegmatites yielded stunning pink and green crystals, and the Empress Dowager Cixi of China bought tons of Californian pink tourmaline, which was carved and prized at the Chinese court. Tourmaline was long confused with ruby, emerald, and sapphire. Today it is recognized as the modern birthstone of October, alongside opal, and the gem of the 8th wedding anniversary.
meaning: Tourmaline is the stone of balance and protection, and its rainbow of colors lets it speak to every chakra. Practitioners associate black tourmaline with grounding and shielding, pink with love, green with growth, and blue with calm communication. Because of its electrical properties, the stone is traditionally said to polarize and balance energies, drawing away what is draining and bringing in steadiness. People use tourmaline to calm worry, to feel safe in busy settings, and to nurture creativity. It is also a stone of self-acceptance, encouraging you to embrace every color of your personality. Multi-color tourmaline is used for aligning the chakras and bringing a sense of wholeness.
howToUse: Choose the color for your intention: black for protection, pink for heart work, green for growth, blue for communication. Place a raw tourmaline crystal on a desk or windowsill. Hold a stone in each hand during meditation to feel balance. Wear a pendant or ring to keep its energy near you. Use multicolor or watermelon tourmaline in chakra layouts, from root to crown. In a grid, set tourmaline at the corners as a protective border around clear quartz. Give tourmaline to a friend who needs encouragement and steadiness.
care: Tourmaline is durable at Mohs 7 to 7.5, but its prismatic crystals can be brittle and some gem stones have fractures. Wash with lukewarm soapy water and a soft cloth. Avoid ultrasonic cleaners with fractured or heavily included stones. Cleanse by running water, moonlight, sound, smoke, or earth. Most tourmaline tolerates sunlight, though pink stones can fade over long exposures, so keep colored stones out of prolonged strong sun. Store apart from harder gems to prevent scratches.
identify: Tourmaline forms striated, rounded-triangular prisms, and the stripes run along the length. Gem stones show strong pleochroism, changing color from different angles. Look-alikes include emerald, ruby, peridot, and glass. Tourmaline is often heated or irradiated to improve pink and red colors, and some blue or paraiba stones are heat treated. Black tourmaline can be mistaken for obsidian or black glass; tourmaline has striations and a fracture that is not conchoidal. A lab can confirm origin and treatment for expensive stones.
